rows.teaches: when a process becomes orphaned, it is reparented to the nearest still living ancestor subreaper, so a subreaper sees descendants whose parent has exited; the page states the rule, not how a signal reaches a descendant that left its process group

rows.scope: open(2)'s access modes and open-time effects, for whether an O_RDWR open is a pure read input
rows.anchor: §DESCRIPTION, O_TRUNC entry in the file creation flags list @ Linux man-pages 6.19 (footer 2026-02-08), fetched 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: O_RDWR requests read/write, and O_TRUNC truncates the file at open whenever the access mode allows writing, so an O_RDWR open with O_TRUNC is a write-capable input, not a pure read

rows.scope: supersedes S072's teaches: what an O_RDWR open is, without the O_TRUNC overstatement
rows.anchor: §DESCRIPTION access-mode paragraph ("These request opening the file read-only, write-only, or read/write, respectively.") and O_TRUNC entry @ Linux man-pages 6.19, re-opened 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: supersedes S072 — O_RDWR requests read/write access, so an O_RDWR open is write-capable and is not recorded as a pure read input; O_TRUNC truncates only an existing regular file (ignored for FIFOs/terminals, otherwise unspecified), so S072's "whenever the access mode allows writing" overstated the page

rows.scope: Linux setsid(2) session and process-group semantics for a caller that leaves its group
rows.anchor: §DESCRIPTION ¶2 and §ERRORS EPERM @ man-pages 6.19 (footer date 2026-06-05), fetched 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: the caller becomes the only process in a new process group and a new session, distinct from its old group; a group-directed signal sent to the old group does not reach it [INFERENCE: follows from the distinct group ID; killpg is not named on this page]; setsid fails with EPERM for a process group leader, so the escaping process must fork and let the child call setsid

rows.scope: Grammar-level meaning of import and export section entries in the binary format, for reading `inspect-wasm-artifact` and `compare-wasm-interfaces` results; not validation or instantiation semantics
rows.anchor: Page title `WebAssembly 3.0 (2026-10-20)`, HTML sha256 `5d1afa388503fd2fdf743e6e339c5fe8e969f3c910b8c62ca59b9e130f89df8f` fetched 2026-10-20; reST `document/core/binary/modules.rst` at commit `a6ed9b2b5f266953872660b1b9ad95d7ca1c4515`, `Indices` (rst:48), Import and Export sections
rows.teaches: An import entry is module name + field name + external type; an export entry is a name + external index with no type, so export signatures come from the index spaces, not the export entry

rows.scope: The documented Arch doctrine that partial upgrades are unsupported, scoped to package-manager advice rather than host state
rows.anchor: § Partial upgrades are unsupported; revision oldid 885170, last edited 2026-09-07T06:06:18Z; page opened 2026-10-20

rows.scope: journal seek to a cursor position and next-closest fallback
rows.anchor: sd_journal_seek_cursor page, Description: "If no entry matching the specified cursor is found the call will seek to the next closest entry (in terms of time) instead."; systemd 262 page accessed 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: A seek to an absent cursor lands on the next closest entry in time, and seeking does not by itself make that entry current.

rows.scope: journal entry-identity test after a seek, distinct from cursor-string comparison
rows.anchor: sd_journal_test_cursor page, Description: "the same entry might be referred to by multiple different cursor strings"; systemd 262 page accessed 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: Cursor strings do not uniquely identify an entry, so string comparison is not an identity test; sd_journal_test_cursor verifies the sought entry after a seek. No deduplication or completeness is implied.

rows.scope: the IPv6 loopback address and the IPv4-mapped address form; not `/proc` output format and not any kernel's printing
rows.anchor: §2.5.3 The Loopback Address, line 474; §2.5.5.2 IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Address, lines 548-552, layout diagram at line 570 (80 zero bits, 16 one bits, 32-bit IPv4 address); raw .txt sha256 4d58dff6b432d5d524bf3a3b7f0337a4177fa65f92ed72f2a92e97b471de48b2
rows.teaches: `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` is the loopback address `::1` (an exact /128); an IPv4-mapped address has 80 zero bits, then `FFFF`, then the IPv4 address, so `::ffff:127.0.0.0/104` is exactly 127.0.0.0/8 mapped.

rows.scope: JSON number grammar: whether NaN and Infinity are valid JSON numbers
rows.anchor: §6 Numbers, sentence before the `number` grammar @ RFC 8259, December 2017 (obsoletes RFC 7159), fetched 2026-10-20
rows.teaches: numeric values the number grammar cannot represent, such as Infinity and NaN, are not permitted in JSON, so a registry timeout_s that is NaN or Infinity is outside the grammar; §6 does not say what a parser must do with them [INFERENCE: refusing it is a design choice]
